title: RE+ 2026 Recap: Power, Permitting, and M&A
summary: What developers said at RE+ 2026 about speed to power, distributed compute, grid data and M&A.
body_markdown:
It wasn't too different to what we're hearing across the industry and what we've been hearing the past couple of years at RE+, but speed to power is still the biggest thing we're hearing. Bridge solutions, anything that will get you megawatts sooner, whether they're grid connected or not. Behind-the-meter plays are still incredibly important in finding creative ways to get power online sooner. So whether it's purely behind the meter with solar and renewables on a large load site, or if solar and BESS play a bridge role until grid connection in 2030, when megawatts are available, that's still a big theme we're hearing across the industry. And then one thing that, I think, is coming up more frequently and wasn't as prevalent last year is distributed compute. So we're shifting from hearing about these gigawatt data center campuses that require a tremendous amount of effort and power to get online towards smaller data center campuses. There was a bit of a shift towards the 100 to 300 megawatt range, but now even smaller, at the distribution level. So distributed compute: edge data centers for inference as opposed to training, in the 5 to 20 megawatt range, whether it's grid connected or, again, a behind-the-meter play, is something we're really hearing. With regards to what I just mentioned, if we take distributed compute, for example, it's just education. It's kind of a net new compute play that hasn't existed before. So without precedent, a barrier to entry is just learning how to do it properly. And then just reliance on good, clean data. If you're making large investments and decisions that have to be made swiftly, what source of truth can you rely on? That's still a barrier to entry, whether it's grid data, how you're assessing power at the point of interconnection or at the substation where you're trying to interconnect, all the way down to: is there going to be a moratorium imposed on battery storage at the site I'm trying to develop? Knowing what the source of truth is, it's achievable, but still a barrier to entry for most developers. I think generally, and this is my personal read, it's net positive for renewables. I think with the incoming administration and what will shake out in the next two years, it will likely be tailwinds for the renewables industry as opposed to headwinds. But energy demand is still largely driven by compute and data centers. In that regard, there's been more local opposition and more and more opposition at the state level to data centers across the country. Although nothing is definitive yet, a proposed moratorium doesn't necessarily mean it will be a moratorium. In some cases, having stricter requirements for permits and how you connect to the grid is actually a good thing for the industry. It forces the developers to think a bit more thoroughly about how they're developing a project, so it gets up and running in the correct way that's beneficial to a community, and that obviously has downstream effects on how those sites are powered. Although there seems to be more opposition towards data centers, everything we're hearing is that load growth is not slowing down. In fact, you need compute now more than ever. So that enables more creative ways to get data centers and compute centers built. And that's what's pulling capital and talent across the industry. So that load growth is pulling talented people from renewables towards those data center developers in a lot of cases. The teams have to be a bit more capital efficient now. They have to be more careful with their resources. At the beginning of, I think, the data center boom, it was a bit of a spray-and-pray approach. Let's allocate a ton of capital to as many projects as we can and see what lands. But now, three or four years in, we're seeing hyperscalers, neoclouds and energy developers be much more capital efficient and find the best opportunities to keep taking forward with leaner and leaner teams as a lot of the manual work gets automated. So these are challenges the industry as a whole is facing, whether it's on the renewable energy development side or on the load side, if you're trying to withdraw from the grid. Stale grid data across the board, whether it's injection or withdrawal. Knowing what base cases you're working with, knowing what utility documents you're running your modeling assumptions on, is incredibly important to have the right idea when you're approaching an interconnection application. So stale grid data is still a huge barrier to entry and challenge on the developer side. And there are still far too many sites failing in late-stage development for critical flaws that could have been picked up earlier. Whether that's a change in a conditional use permit, where one of the steps in the application was missed in the early stages, or on the grid side, where you made modeling assumptions, submitted your interconnection application, waited six to nine months for your results, and then found out there's maybe only 20 megawatts when you assumed there were 200 megawatts. One of the ways we think the industry can clean a lot of this up is going directly to the sources and having data freshness. So at Paces, we're developing an Interconnection Intel portal where all of this lives, whether it's the base cases or the utility planning documentation, from the ISO level down to the utility and, in some cases, the co-op level, and be able to run power flow studies and get a great understanding of what those utility studies would look like on cleaner, refreshed data. Same goes for permitting pathways as well as community sentiment. So in terms of data freshness and traceability, we collect every possible public data source that's available. We also have some proprietary datasets that are either gated at the federal level, which we've applied for and been approved for at the ISO base case level, or proprietary datasets we've built. And the way we keep that data fresh is, one, going directly to the source, but then manually verifying. And by manual, I mean picking up the phone and calling the utilities, calling the town boards, for example, going directly to any community groups that are popping up from a sentiment pushback perspective and talking to those folks directly. That gives us a great idea of how the community is feeling. And this is done through expert review by former developers. On the Development-as-a-Service team, we have folks who have worked in the renewable energy and power industries, at utilities, as consultants who have done this job, boots on the ground, in prior roles, and are now bringing that expertise to Paces and applying the same type of diligence directly to the sources. M&A is becoming more and more relevant. It has been for the last few years, but now more than ever, because as projects face more opposition from the sentiment perspective and potentially interconnection delays on larger projects, instead of greenfielding projects, you often turn to acquiring portfolios of projects or assets on their own, which gives us a great opportunity at Paces to diligence M&A opportunities. So what is most critical here? One is understanding what the seller actually has in their data room. What are they selling? Is it a real asset? And the second thing is speed. Another word we heard across RE+ and have been hearing in the industry is velocity. How many sites can I screen at scale, and how quickly can I get to a go or no-go decision? The way we do this is we match Paces data. We take an objective read of the site, get an understanding of what has actually been done there, and then we look at the data room the seller is providing. So we go and find the relevant documentation, do a full sweep of what is being presented, and then reconcile the two to give you a clean read of whether the project has a pathway forward or not. If so, what is left outstanding in the development steps? What are the big risks that could tank the project? We flag those in under five business days. In the same way we do diligence for net new sites, we do this for existing assets. For those who don't know, they do second-life batteries, from electric vehicles down to laptop batteries. Anything that's a lithium-ion battery, they give a second life and repurpose. They also have an energy team that's deploying battery storage at scale with these second-life batteries, and Paces has had the opportunity to work with them for over a year now. So stopping by their booth and seeing projects Paces has helped support and develop actually get constructed, and seeing those live projects, was quite special. **The short answer:** Speed to power was still the top theme at RE+ 2026 in Las Vegas, but the projects chasing it are getting smaller. Distributed data centers of 5 to 20 megawatts (MW), built for AI inference and often paired with behind-the-meter or bridge power, came up far more than last year. Two weeks before the show, voters restricted data centers in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, which pushed permitting and community risk to the front of site screening. With tax credit deadlines approaching and teams staying lean, developers have less room for sites that won’t make it, especially when they could have caught grid or permitting issues sooner.


I spent most of RE+ week speaking with developers, independent power producers (IPPs) and data center teams. The demand signal was the strongest I've heard. Interest in 1 to 15 MW projects has gone from close to zero to more than the market can supply in about six months, driven largely by mid-tier AI cloud providers that have chip allocations and need power by 2027. They will pay a premium for it. What changed is how much risk developers are willing to carry to get there.


## **What were developers talking about at RE+ 2026?**


Speed to power, again. What's new is the scale: the conversation has moved from gigawatt campuses, to 100 to 300 MW sites, and now down to distributed compute at the distribution level.


- **Bridge and behind-the-meter power.** Anything that gets megawatts online sooner, grid-connected or not, is on the table. That can mean solar and battery energy storage (BESS) behind the meter on a large load site, or solar and storage serving as a bridge until a grid connection opens up around 2030. The engineers I talked to were more skeptical of gigawatt-scale onsite power. Their concerns were reliability, too little storage to handle harmonics, generation that can't ramp, and late design changes that strand equipment.
- [Distributed compute](https://www.paces.com/data-center-developers) **.** This wasn't a big topic last year. Now we hear about it constantly: edge data centers of 5 to 20 MW, built for inference rather than training, on existing industrial and renewable sites. The main barrier is education. It's a new kind of compute project with little precedent, so teams are still learning how to do it properly.
- **Powered land and large load tariffs.** Developers are shifting from standalone storage toward powered land, and some are hiring dedicated powered-land leads. Some new large load tariffs let utilities curtail big loads for set hours each year, so onsite backup is part of the plan from day one.


## **How did the 2026 midterm elections affect renewable and data center development?**


The clearest signal for developers came from local ballots. On November 3, voters favored limits on data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures, according to[Ballotpedia](https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/11/06/voters-favored-limiting-data-center-development-in-40-of-41-local-ballot-measures-on-nov-3/) , including five full bans (in California, Florida and Ohio) and three six-month moratoriums, all in Maine.


The results didn't follow party lines. Political scientist Barbara Trish, in a piece[Fortune](https://fortune.com/2026/11/13/voters-data-centers-ballot-measures-midterms/) republished, found the restrictions passed by an average margin of 49 points, in communities as different as Edgewater, Florida and Alhambra, California. A tracker we maintain holds about 1,200 local moratorium and ban records, and as of mid-October our permitting data flagged 239 jurisdictions with an active data center moratorium.


My personal read is that the results are net positive for renewables: with the incoming administration, there will likely be tailwinds for the industry rather than headwinds. That doesn't mean every proposal becomes law. A proposed moratorium doesn't necessarily become a moratorium, and in some cases stricter requirements for permits and grid connections are good for the industry. They force developers to think through how a project gets built in a way that benefits the community, and that affects how those sites are powered, renewables included.


The practical change for our customers: permitting and community risk now come up at the start of site screening, not at the end.


## **What macroeconomic forces are shaping power development right now?**


Load growth. Even with more opposition to data centers, everything we hear says demand for compute isn't slowing, and it's pulling capital and people toward data center development.


1. **Talent is moving.** Service providers are moving people from renewable developers to data center developers.
2. **Capital is moving up in scale.** Investors who used to back only early and mid-stage development are now looking at utility-scale developers, whose capital needs keep growing.
3. **Tax credit deadlines are close.** Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, wind and solar projects that didn't begin construction by July 4, 2026 must be[placed in service by December 31, 2027](https://www.thetaxadviser.com/issues/2026/feb/navigating-safe-harbor-rules-for-solar-and-wind-sec-48e-facilities.html) to claim the Section 45Y and 48E credits. Storage and other technologies have a longer runway, but many solar and wind projects are now racing the end-of-2027 deadline.
4. **Teams are leaner.** Early in the data center boom, a lot of capital went to as many projects as possible to see which ones worked. Three or four years in, hyperscalers, neoclouds and energy developers are far more selective, pursuing the best opportunities with smaller teams as more of the manual work gets automated. One storage developer told us they want 70 sites under control by the end of 2027 with the team they have today.


## **Why do so few sites make it through development?**


About 19% of projects that requested interconnection between 2000 and 2020 had reached commercial operation by the end of 2025, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory's[Queued Up report](https://emp.lbl.gov/queues) . Many of the rest drop out late, on issues that were knowable early. Utility planning cases are out of date the day they're released, hosting capacity maps lag behind the grid, and early screens often skip permitting and interconnection checks.


The failure usually shows up months later. A team makes its modeling assumptions, submits an interconnection application, waits six to nine months for results, and learns there are 20 MW available where it assumed 200. Or a step in a conditional use permit application was missed early and surfaces at the end. On top of that, learning how much power a site can get often means multiple applications and large study fees to transmission owners.


The fix is to go to the source and keep the data fresh. When our development team builds a permit matrix, we check every public data source and then call the authority having jurisdiction (AHJ), whether that's a town, a county or a state agency. We join calls with utilities, planning boards and public utility commissions (PUCs). Those conversations also tell you how town hall meetings are going and how planning boards think about development. Once you have a direct line to those people, you have a much better sense of whether your project will get built.


## **How is M&A changing clean energy development?**


Acquisitions are replacing some greenfield development. As larger projects face more community opposition and interconnection delays, many teams buy portfolios or single assets instead of starting from scratch, and they want answers quickly.


Buyers start with two questions. First, what does the seller have in the data room, and is it a real asset? Second, how fast can I get to a go or no-go decision? Another word we kept hearing at RE+ was velocity: buyers want[gap and fatal-flaw analysis](https://www.paces.com/post/ma-diligence-reports-what-buyers-need-to-know-before-they-commit) within the first five to ten days of a data room opening.


We also heard that smaller buyers feel underserved, with thin coverage and mostly automated output. They want senior, human-led diligence with automation behind it. Many buyers pay one vendor for early screening and another for full diligence and want to consolidate. Lenders want an independent second read of the data room to catch buried red flags before investment committee.


## **The best moment of the week at RE+**


The most interesting booth I visited was Redwood Materials. Redwood gives lithium-ion batteries a second life, from electric vehicle packs down to laptop batteries, and its energy team deploys battery storage at scale using those second-life batteries. Paces has worked with Redwood for more than a year.


I walked up to their booth and recognized the project on display: a site our team found and helped develop, now built. Seeing a project go from a screening result to steel in the ground is the reason we do this work.


## **My take**


AI compute is still driving most new energy demand. What's changing is the shape of it, from gigawatt-scale campuses toward smaller, distributed projects, and the bar for diligence that comes with it. The challenges around building data centers have downstream effects on renewable energy, but overall I came away from RE+ positive about where the industry is headed.


If you see it differently,[reach out to me on LinkedIn](https://www.linkedin.com/in/tonywagler/) . I'd like to hear what you're seeing.

## Frequently Asked Questions


### What were the biggest themes at RE+ 2026?


Speed to power was the top theme, followed by bridge and behind-the-meter power, distributed compute (5 to 20 MW data centers for AI inference), powered land and large load tariffs. Developers also focused on local opposition after the November 3 ballot results and on doing more with lean teams.


### What is distributed compute in data center development?


Distributed compute is a model in which smaller data centers, typically 5 to 20 MW, are built at the distribution level for AI inference rather than training. They often sit on existing industrial or renewable sites and can be grid-connected or powered behind the meter.


### How did the 2026 midterm ballot measures affect data center development?


Voters favored limits on data center development in 40 of 41 local ballot measures on November 3, 2026, according to[Ballotpedia](https://news.ballotpedia.org/2026/11/06/voters-favored-limiting-data-center-development-in-40-of-41-local-ballot-measures-on-nov-3/) , including five full bans and three six-month moratoriums. As a result, developers now assess permitting and community risk at the start of site screening.


### What are the tax credit deadlines for solar and wind projects?


Under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, wind and solar projects that did not begin construction by July 4, 2026 must be placed in service by December 31, 2027 to qualify for the Section 45Y and 48E credits. Storage and other technologies have a longer runway.


### Why do so few power projects make it through development?


About 19% of projects that requested interconnection from 2000 to 2020 reached commercial operation, according to Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory. Many of the rest drop out late on issues that trace back to stale or incomplete early data: outdated utility planning cases, low-quality hosting capacity maps, and screens that skip permitting and interconnection checks. A team can wait six to nine months for interconnection results and find 20 MW where it assumed 200 MW.


### What do buyers want from M&A diligence on power projects?


Speed and a clear verdict. Buyers want gap and fatal-flaw analysis within the first five to ten days of a data room opening, senior human-led review backed by automation, and one vendor for both early screening and full diligence.
